title: Out of the Sea
sources: Every claim is checked against episodes/dubai-islands/research.md (R1-R7).
Own measurement R1: Landsat 7 22 May 2001 vs Landsat 8 24 Sep 2026, NDWI > 0 water; 62.7 km2 became land, 4.9 km2 water, net ~58 km2 (tools/dubai_numbers.py). Manhattan ~59 km2 land.
Own calculation: 92,234,000 m3 / (105 m x 68 m) = 12.9 km.

youtube.title: In 25 Years, Dubai Built a Manhattan in the Sea
youtube.description:
In May 2001 the coast of Dubai was a straight line of sand. By September 2026 it had two palm-shaped islands, a map of the world made of about 300 islands, and a fourth archipelago. We measured the new land ourselves from Landsat images: about 58 square kilometres, roughly the size of Manhattan. How it was built, the 2009 debt crisis that froze it, whether it is sinking, and why the building has started again.

Real Landsat and Copernicus Sentinel-2 images, NASA astronaut photographs and our own measurements.
youtube.pinned_comment: Would you live on land that was open sea 25 years ago? Yes, no, or only on the first palm?

paragraphs.text: This is the coast of Dubai on May 22nd, 2001: a straight line of sand, and open sea. Now watch the same coast in September 2026.

shots.on_screen_text: Real satellite images · Landsat 7 and Landsat 8

paragraphs.text: Two palm trees, each several kilometres across. A map of the world, made of about three hundred islands. And to the north, a fourth group of islands, still mostly empty.
We measured it ourselves. Comparing the two satellite images, about 58 square kilometres of new land has appeared off this coast in 25 years. That is roughly the land area of Manhattan.

shots.on_screen_text: New land since May 2001 · our measurement

stat.label: of new land off Dubai, May 2001 to September 2026
stat.note: Roughly the land area of Manhattan (about 59 km²)
stat.source: Our measurement: Landsat 7 and 8 water masks, ±10 %

stat.label: about 59 km² of land, for comparison

paragraphs.text: It was built from sand pumped off the seabed and rock from sixteen quarries. It survived a debt crisis that nearly broke the city. And now, after more than a decade of silence, the second palm is being built again.

shots.on_screen_text: March 2003: the first palm, still bare sand

paragraphs.text: So is this the boldest engineering of the century, or the most expensive sandcastle ever built? To answer that, you have to start with what Dubai was running out of.

shots.on_screen_text: July 2026, from the International Space Station

shots.subtitle: How Dubai built new land, and what it cost

ask.text: Boldest engineering of the century, or a very expensive sandcastle?

paragraphs.text: It was not sand. It was oil. Dubai's oil output peaked in the early 1990s, at roughly 410,000 barrels a day, and it has been falling ever since.

stat.label: barrels a day: Dubai's oil output at its peak, around 1991

shots.on_screen_text: Oil output falling since the early 1990s

paragraphs.text: One estimate puts it at 50 to 70 thousand barrels a day today. By 2016, oil and gas made up only about one percent of the emirate's economy.

stat.label: barrels a day today (estimate)
of Dubai's economy came from oil and gas in 2016

paragraphs.text: Dubai had bet its future on trade, flights and tourists instead. But a tourist city needs beaches, and Dubai had only about 72 kilometres of natural shoreline.
And the city was filling up fast. In 2000, Dubai had fewer than a million residents. On September 8th, 2025, its official population clock passed four million.

stat.label: Dubai residents in 2000
stat.source: Dubai Statistics Center, via Gulf News / Khaleej Times

stat.label: residents on 8 September 2025: the four-million mark
stat.source: Dubai Statistics Center population clock, via Gulf News

paragraphs.text: The answer was to draw new coastline in the shape of a palm tree. A trunk, sixteen fronds and a crescent around them. Every frond is a long, thin beach, and every beach is waterfront property.
How much beach does that shape buy? We traced the edges of all the new islands in the 2026 satellite image. Around their edges, they add more than 500 kilometres of shoreline. Dubai started with 72.

shots.on_screen_text: Our measurement: the outlines of the new land

stat.label: of new shoreline around the islands, by our rough count
stat.note: Pixel-traced outlines (657 km) overstate a little; the natural coast is about 72 km

paragraphs.text: Construction started in June 2001. In March 2003, an astronaut on the International Space Station photographed the palm while it was still bare sand.

stat.label: Palm Jumeirah's land reclamation begins

paragraphs.text: Every grain of it came from the bottom of the Gulf. Dredging ships sucked the sand up offshore and sprayed it towards the shape in high arcs, a technique engineers call rainbowing.

stat.label: dredgers spraying sand into place in high arcs

paragraphs.text: Why not use the desert, which is right next door? Because wind-blown desert sand is the wrong kind. Its grains are worn round by the wind, and round grains do not lock together. Builders need the angular sand found underwater.

shots.on_screen_text: Desert sand: grains rounded by the wind

stat.label: don't lock together, so desert sand is poor for building
stat.source: UNEP 2014 sand report, as reported; geologists quoted there

paragraphs.text: More than ninety million cubic metres went into this one island. Piled on a football pitch, that sand would make a column about thirteen kilometres high, higher than airliners fly.

stat.label: of sand in Palm Jumeirah (developer's figure)
high: that sand piled on one football pitch

paragraphs.text: Loose sand under water is not ground you can build a villa on. So the engineers pushed vibrating probes into it and jetted water through, shaking the grains until they packed tightly together. The method is called vibro-compaction.

stat.label: vibrating probes and water jets pack the sand

paragraphs.text: To protect the palm from waves, they wrapped it in a crescent breakwater, built from roughly seven million tonnes of rock brought in from sixteen quarries.

stat.label: of rock in the breakwater, from 16 quarries

paragraphs.text: Then the first big problem appeared. The crescent was built as one closed wall, and inside it the water stopped moving. The lagoons between the fronds began to go stagnant.
The fix was to cut two openings into the crescent, each about a hundred metres wide. With the tide flowing through them, the water inside is now renewed in about two weeks.

shots.on_screen_text: Two ~100 m openings in the breakwater

stat.label: for the water inside the crescent to renew

paragraphs.text: At the top of the palm, a resort called Atlantis opened in September 2008. In April 2009, a monorail started carrying passengers up the trunk, the first in the Middle East.

By the end of 2006, five years after the first sand was pumped, the first residents moved in. But the palm was only the opening act. A few kilometres further out, Dubai had started something far larger.
Work on The World began in 2003: about three hundred islands, arranged as a map of the continents, four to six kilometres off the coast.
It took about three hundred and twenty million cubic metres of sand, three and a half times as much as the first palm.

chart.title: Sand used
chart.source: Palm Jumeirah website (archived); NASA Earth Observatory / Nakheel

stat.label: as much sand as Palm Jumeirah

paragraphs.text: Around it runs a breakwater about twenty-seven kilometres long, made of some thirty-seven million tonnes of rock, according to NASA. The last stone was laid on January 10th, 2008.

shots.photo: File:Artificial Archipelagos, Dubai, United Arab Emirates ISS022-E-024940 lrg (cropped to The World).jpg

stat.label: of rock in a 27-km breakwater
the last stone of The World's breakwater

paragraphs.text: The plan was to sell the islands one by one, to developers and to the very rich: your own island, a short boat ride from the city.

shots.photo: File:Dubai 2011-03-23 – The World – Artificial Islands – America, Atlantic and Africa - العالم - الجزر الاصطناعية - الأمريكية ، والمحيط الأطلسي وأفريقيا - panoramio.jpg
File:Looking out over Dubais The World artificial islands (5373745497).jpg

ask.text: Would you buy your own empty island a boat ride from Dubai?

paragraphs.text: By 2011, Nakheel said about seventy percent of the islands had been sold. But reports at the time said that all but one were still uninhabited, and that one was a showpiece island owned by the ruler of Dubai: Greenland.

stat.label: of The World's islands sold by 2011, Nakheel said
islands inhabited, according to 2011 reports

shots.on_screen_text: 2011 reports: the one inhabited island, Greenland

paragraphs.text: That same year, a company with a contract on the islands told a Dubai tribunal that The World was eroding, slowly falling back into the sea. The tribunal rejected the claim. Nakheel said its own surveys had found no erosion that needed new sand.

shots.photo: File:Dubai 2011-03-23 – The World – Artificial Islands – America, Atlantic and Africa - العالم - الجزر الاصطناعية - الأمريكية ، والمحيط الأطلسي وأفريقيا - panoramio.jpg

shots.on_screen_text: The claim: the islands are eroding

stat.label: a tribunal rejects the claim that The World is eroding

shots.photo: File:Looking out over Dubais The World artificial islands (5373745497).jpg

paragraphs.text: Most of them are still empty today. And the reason has very little to do with sand.
By 2008, Dubai's developers had borrowed heavily to build. Then the global financial crisis hit, and buyers vanished.

stat.label: global financial crisis: buyers vanish

paragraphs.text: On November 25th, 2009, the state-owned group Dubai World asked its creditors for a standstill: a pause on about 26 billion dollars of debt, most of it linked to Nakheel, the company building the islands.

stat.label: asks creditors to pause its debts, 25 November 2009
of debt Dubai World asked to pause
the state-owned developer of the islands, part of Dubai World

paragraphs.text: Nakheel had an Islamic bond worth three and a half billion dollars falling due on December 14th. Markets waited to see whether Dubai would default.

stat.label: Nakheel's Islamic bond, due 14 December 2009

paragraphs.text: On that same day, neighbouring Abu Dhabi stepped in with 10 billion dollars. About four billion of it went straight to repay Nakheel's bond.

stat.label: of Abu Dhabi's $10 billion repaid the bond that day

paragraphs.text: Three weeks later, Dubai opened the tallest building in the world. Until the ceremony it was called Burj Dubai. On the day, it was renamed Burj Khalifa, after the ruler of Abu Dhabi.

stat.label: Burj Dubai opens as Burj Khalifa

paragraphs.text: In parts of the city, property prices had fallen by nearly half in a year.

stat.label: fall in property prices in parts of Dubai, 2009
stat.source: Reports at the time (Mail & Guardian, AP)

paragraphs.text: Dubai was rescued. Its islands were not. Work on the second palm, Palm Jebel Ali, stopped. Its sand was already in place in May 2008. Now look at the same palm in October 2022.
Fourteen years, and almost nothing had changed: bare fronds, and no houses.

The third palm, Palm Deira, had been planned at roughly eight times the size of the first. It was redesigned in 2008, shrunk and renamed Deira Islands in 2013, and renamed again in 2022: Dubai Islands.

stat.label: Palm Deira's planned size against Palm Jumeirah
Palm Deira → Deira Islands (2013) → Dubai Islands (2022)

paragraphs.text: And while the projects stood still, a rumour spread around the world: the islands were sinking.
In 2009, newspapers reported that a satellite study had found the first palm sinking by five millimetres a year.

stat.label: the sinking rate reported in 2009
stat.source: 2009 press reports of a Fugro NPA study

paragraphs.text: The company behind the measurements, Fugro NPA, said its findings had been taken out of context. Early movements, it said, were under a centimetre a year: the normal settling of new ground.

shots.on_screen_text: Fugro NPA: the company behind the measurements

stat.label: Fugro NPA on the 2009 reports
early settling, normal for new land, according to Fugro NPA

paragraphs.text: The developer went further. Nakheel said the island would settle by at most 25 millimetres over a whole century.

shots.on_screen_text: Nakheel: at most 25 mm in 100 years

stat.label: at most, in 100 years: Nakheel's settlement estimate

paragraphs.text: We looked for a published, peer-reviewed measurement of how fast the palms are moving today, and we did not find one. Some settling is normal for reclaimed land, and we could not find public data showing more than that.

The bigger cost may be underwater. Reports at the time described dredging that clouded the water and buried reefs and oyster beds. Nakheel acknowledged that its projects had covered reefs, and said it would build artificial ones.

stat.label: buried under dredged sediment, reports said in 2005

paragraphs.text: A 2006 study at Duke University found both sides. The island buried marine life and changed how sand moves along the shore. But its rock breakwater also became a new habitat.

stat.label: buried habitat and changed sand drift, but new life on the rocks

ask.text: Is new life on the rocks worth the reefs buried under the sand?

paragraphs.text: Fifteen years after the crash, the money came back.
Today the first palm is one of the most expensive addresses in the city. In the first eight months of 2026, it led Dubai in home sales above ten million dollars.

stat.label: area for Dubai home sales above $10 million, January-August 2026

paragraphs.text: In 2023, Palm Jebel Ali was relaunched. Its first villas sold out within hours.

stat.label: the first Palm Jebel Ali villas sold out, September 2023

paragraphs.text: In 2024, the state-owned Dubai Holding took over Nakheel. And in April 2026, Nakheel awarded contracts worth 3.5 billion dirhams, about 950 million dollars, to build 544 villas on the palm.

stat.label: took over Nakheel in 2024
of contracts for 544 villas, April 2026
on Palm Jebel Ali, contracts April 2026

paragraphs.text: Compare December 2022 with September 2026, and you can see the work spreading along the fronds.
The first homes are due from late 2026 into 2027. Finished, Palm Jebel Ali will be about twice the size of the first palm, with more than 100 kilometres of coastline.

stat.label: first handovers, continuing into 2027
Palm Jumeirah's size, with more than 100 km of coastline

paragraphs.text: The World is a different story. Its most advanced project, the Heart of Europe, was meant to be finished in 2026. The target has slipped to the end of 2027, and most of the other islands are still bare sand.

stat.label: the new target for the Heart of Europe

paragraphs.text: And Dubai isn't finished. In April 2026, Semafor reported that the city is betting on even more artificial coastline.
Back to where we started. Here is every patch of land that did not exist in May 2001: about 58 square kilometres of it.

shots.on_screen_text: New land since May 2001 · our measurement

paragraphs.text: It was built for beaches and waterfront homes. For a while it looked as if it would sink a city, not the islands. Now the money is back, and the building has started again.
We measure changes like this from orbit in every episode, so if you want to see the next coast we measure, subscribe.
So, would you live on land that was open sea twenty-five years ago?

ask.text: Would you live on land that was open sea 25 years ago?
